title: Fifty-four portions
hookLine: the Torah is divided into weekly portions and finished every year on Simchat Torah

cards: Before streaming, a show came out one episode a week. Nobody could binge it. Everyone saw the same episode on the same night, and the next day at work, people talked about it.
The Torah reading works a little like that, except the week never skips and the audience is spread across the world.
On most Shabbat mornings, a synagogue in Buenos Aires, one in Paris and one in Melbourne are reading the same portion. People even name the week after it.

teach.b: The word is parashah, a portion, a section set apart. The five books of Moses are divided into fifty-four portions, one read each Shabbat, starting in the fall.
Fifty-four is more than the weeks some years have free, since festivals sometimes fall on Shabbat, so in some years two short portions are read together to keep the cycle on time.
Each portion is named for its first important word or two. The first is Bereshit, in the beginning. The second is Noach, Noah.
The third, Lech Lecha, go forth. So Jews will say, this is the week of Noach, the way you might say, it's the week of the big game. A bar or bat mitzvah is often remembered by its portion.

And the cycle ends on a holiday you've met: Simchat Torah, rejoicing in the Torah. That day, the last lines of Deuteronomy are read, the death of Moses, and then, right away, the first lines of Genesis again.
There's dancing with the scrolls. The story never stops; it just starts over. Here's a surprise: it wasn't always one year.
The Talmud mentions that in the land of Israel, people finished the Torah in three years, in smaller pieces. In Babylonia, it was read in one, and the one-year cycle became the common practice.
Some congregations today, especially in the Conservative and Reform movements, read a third of each portion instead, over a three-year cycle.
Either way, the week has a portion, and the portion gives the week its name.

how: Synagogues read the weekly portion on Shabbat morning in an annual cycle that ends and begins again on Simchat Torah; some Conservative and Reform congregations read a triennial cycle.

practice: Think back over the last seven days: if this week were a chapter, what would its first important word be? Not the whole story, just the word that opens it.
Let one come, then look ahead and wonder what the coming week's name might be.

wordCard.voice: Parashah. A portion: one of fifty-four weekly readings, each named for its first words, finished every year on Simchat Torah.
